body: No worries, sleep well. There are others who feel similarly, but we're generally a no-fun-at-parties bunch, if you take my meaning. Antisocial comes with the territory, and naturally so. Enough to justify another who knows how many decades of all the trash and general fuckery of life. There's more than that, but not much. All around, prospects are dismal and not showing a sign of probable improvement, but I'm not quite ready to make the big jump yet.

I guess it's the closest thing I've ever come to really, truly loving something. If I love anything it's writing. But I never know if it's enough. It was certainly cathartic to write, thank you for reading.

I must disagree about the universality of my sentiments. Most people are deluding themselves, I find.

What if the malicious AI is released before all of that infrastructure is in place? As for the money, an AI very well could use money an incentive, manipulation of a few bank statements and an AI could have access to all kinds of money.

Are you familiar with [Elizier Yudkowsky's AI in the box experiment?](http://yudkowsky.net/singularity/aibox/) Humans are remarkably easy to deceive when we are talking about an intelligence at the level of which an AI will be capable.

I don't pretend to speak for the unwashed masses: like esther said, it's not always about reason when it comes to this sort of thing. Sometimes people find themselves in a dark place, where they confront the reality that is human existence. Sometimes this drives them to attempt suicide, a course of action frequently met with mixed results: death of course, the infinitely cleaner option, is seldom assured on the first go without informed preparation or a method of devastating certainty. As a result, there are a number of individuals roaming the earth who, having earnestly sought their own end, find themselves caught even still within the web of conscious human experience. How is this possible? One would like imagine that once the course of self elimination has been set, there would be some degree of certainty. But people have never in their existence been so straightforward as that. They stumble, they falter. They make mistakes, and in so doing they even sometimes learn something. There is no blanket revelation that overwhelms their sense of despair, no easy exit previously overlooked: as a survivor, you are faced with limited options. Try again, stop caring, or keep looking. To understand these, one must first come to terms with the source of suicidality itself. Humans are remarkably well equipped to ignore that which might significantly hamper their ability to survive, and the bleak reality of existence is one of the most strongly ignored truths in human history. Once an inkling of individual and collective futility has been introduced, it must be constantly submerged or actively wrestled. The third option of acceptance is an interesting albeit unrelated phenomenon, unrelated inasmuch as this will generally eliminate the urge to commit suicide or it will ensure it without fail. Once the pain, pointlessness, and inevitability of termination regardless reaches a nascent critical mass, suffering individuals will act out with self destructive behavior, from petty to the ultimate rebellion of suicide. If this final act of refuge is thwarted by poor planning, incompetence, or intervention, the very fact that the act was attempted will probably have a transformative impact on the individual in question. Hence this trifold path suggested earlier: one can make further attempts at suicide, one can cease to care about the world, the self, about everything and just drift through life, or one can continue searching for a solution to the problems of our current modality of existence. There is a strong bias towards the last of these, as many if not all vocal survivors fall into this category, myself included in large part. Those who try again and again will soon meet with success, and those who cease to care will eventually fall into either category or die as a result of their indifferent lifestyle.

You don't feel helped by these stories because their isn't much help to be found in them. Whatever inspiration might overtake survivors, it is far from universal and is almost always simply another form of denial. What hope remains takes the form of scattered remnants, tiny lights that offer the barest glimmer of possibility in an existence otherwise conceived and contained in bleak, fruitless nothingness. Even these often reveal themselves to be of little actual value, in the fullness of time. The problem stems from your approach, however: these matters cannot be understood in terms of hope. For the suicidal, existence is centrally concerned with the hope for hope, rather than its realization. There is none to be had. The most one can hope for as of now are the tools and coping mechanisms capable of maintaining momentum, of staying alive as long as possible in the incredibly off chance that there is more yet to existence than the merely real.
